View Transitions API with HTML-in-canvas

Four experiments with document.startViewTransition(), view-transition-name, element.startViewTransition() and cross-document transitions, each with a <canvas layoutsubtree> in the page. The live transitions page doesn't use this API. This page does.

1. A canvas that draws HTML, inside a view transition

The green area is a canvas. The white card is a child element of the canvas, drawn with drawElementImage() at a slight angle. "Swap layout" changes the grid inside a view transition. Choose which element has a view-transition-name and where the transition starts.

Show the code a canvas with HTML children in a view transition
  1. The markup. The card is a child of the canvas, so the page doesn't paint it. The canvas does.
  2. The names. The canvas is a replaced element, so it can carry a view-transition-name like an image can.
  3. Draw the card. 2D drawElementImage() also sets where clicks on the card land.
  4. Start the transition. startViewTransition() exists on document and, in Chromium 157, on every element.
  • Name on the canvas: works. The old snapshot contains the card as the canvas drew it. The new snapshot is live: the clock in the card keeps counting while the canvas moves and changes size. The canvas gets paint events during the transition.
  • Name on the card: the group moves, the picture is empty. Chromium makes ::view-transition-group(the-card) and animates it between the two places drawElementImage() put the card, but both snapshots are blank. The card only shows inside the canvas cross-fade.
  • Started on the grid element: works, the same as on the document, and the rest of the page stays interactive.
  • Started on the canvas element: the canvas is blank for the length of the transition. A scope takes part in its own transition as view-transition-name: root, and the pseudo-elements that would show its snapshot are inside the canvas, which renders none of its contents.
  • Started on the canvas element with view-transition-name: none on it: the canvas keeps drawing. The transition runs and shows nothing. The tiles jump, because they're outside the scope. Experiment 4 uses this.
  • Started on a drawable child of the canvas: the tab crashes. This is on its own page so that it can't take this one down. A child without the drawable attribute doesn't crash, and can't be drawn.

2. A shader in place of the cross-fade

The box below is a <live-transition> element with a view-transition-name. The view transition moves the box. The old snapshot is hidden and the new one isn't faded, so what shows is the live canvas, and the canvas runs a shader from the first state to the second.

Show the code the view transition moves the box, the canvas draws the change
  1. The markup.
  2. Turn off the cross-fade for this name. The new snapshot of a view transition is live, so a canvas that keeps drawing shows through it.
  3. Prepare the shader first, then start both. Rendering is paused while the update callback runs, so anything that waits for a paint event has to happen before startViewTransition().

3. Between two documents

Two pages opt in with @view-transition { navigation: auto }. Each has a canvas with the same view-transition-name. The second link also passes the old page's canvas pixels to the new page, which burns from them to its own content.

4. A transition scoped to the canvas, drawn by the canvas

The six items below are HTML in a grid, inside one canvas. "Shuffle" calls canvas.startViewTransition() and reorders them. The browser makes a group for each named item but shows none of them, because they're inside the canvas. The canvas reads each group's animation as a clock and draws the item on its way from the old box to the new one, with an arc and a turn that a group animation couldn't add to live HTML.

FourHTML text

Show the code CSS times the move, the canvas draws it
  1. The markup. One drawable wrapper holds the grid, so CSS grid lays the items out. Each item has a view-transition-name.
  2. The clock. The group's own keyframes are replaced by one that animates a registered custom property from 0 to 1. Duration, easing and per-item delay stay in CSS.
  3. Start the transition on the canvas. Measure the old boxes first. The new ones are the layout after the callback.
  4. Draw each item. The nine-argument drawElementImage() copies one item's rectangle out of the wrapper's picture to wherever the clock says it is.
  • Works, with the canvas doing the geometry. In a transition scoped to the canvas, every ::view-transition-group() reports its size but sits at 0,0, so the positions come from offsetLeft and offsetTop before and after the change. The timing comes from the group animations.
  • The page stays interactive and other scoped transitions can run at the same time: press "Swap layout" in experiment 1 with "the grid element" during a slow shuffle.
  • The items are live while they move (the clocks count), but clicks reach them only at rest. The wrapper has one hit box, and the pieces are drawn apart.
  • Direct children of a canvas don't flow. Each drawable child is laid out alone at the canvas origin, which is why the grid is one child and the items are its children.

Findings

  • A drawable canvas takes part in a view transition as one picture. Its snapshot is the canvas bitmap, HTML children included. The new snapshot is live, so the canvas can keep animating under ::view-transition-new().
  • A canvas child can't be its own transition element. It gets a group with the right box and no picture. To move one element on its own, give it its own canvas and name that canvas.
  • The old and new snapshots can't be read from script. There is no call that hands ::view-transition-old() to a canvas or a shader. A shader transition has to keep both states itself (two live elements, or an ElementImage taken before the change) and switch the cross-fade off.
  • Work that waits for a paint event must be done before startViewTransition(). The canvas gets no paint event while the update callback is pending.
  • Element-scoped transitions (Chrome 147 and later). On an ancestor of the canvas they work as on the document. On the canvas they blank it, unless the canvas has view-transition-name: none: then it keeps drawing and the transition is an invisible set of group animations that the canvas can read. On a drawable child of the canvas they crash the renderer in Chromium 157.
  • Inside a canvas-scoped transition, group sizes are right and group positions are all 0,0. In a document transition the group of a canvas child has the position that drawElementImage() gave it.
  • Between documents, a named canvas cross-fades like any other element. An ElementImage can't follow the navigation, so a shader between two documents needs pixels: the old page stores a picture of its canvas, and the new page draws from that picture to its live content.

Not tried yet

  • Run the items of experiment 4 through a WebGL or WebGPU shader (trails, bending) with the same CSS clock.
  • Nested scopes: a scoped transition on the grid element with a canvas-scoped one inside it.
  • Navigation API navigate with intercept() and a shader transition for a single-page app's route changes.
  • view-transition-class and nested groups (view-transition-group: contain) with one canvas per list item.
  • A page-wide shader: put the whole page in one canvas, so that a transition between any two states is drawn by the canvas and the View Transitions API is only used for timing.
